title: The Slope and the Turn: When a Vehicle Tips, the Speed a Curve Allows, and a Tilt Estimate That Is Not Fooled by a Turn

questions.question: What most often tips a ground vehicle over?
options: A slope it was told to climb straight up
A sensor fault that hides an obstacle
A strong wind from the side
A turn at a speed its geometry does not allow, or a payload that raised its centre of gravity
questions.explanation: The sideways acceleration in a turn is the speed squared times the curvature, and what the vehicle can take falls as its centre of gravity rises.

questions.question: A payload lifts the centre of gravity from 0.3 m to 0.5 m on a track of 0.5 m. What happens to the tipping acceleration?
options: It falls from 8.18 to 4.91 m/s^2, 40 percent less, and the slope it tips on from 39.8 to 26.6 degrees
It halves, from 8.18 to 4.09 m/s2, and the slope from 39.8 to 19.9 degrees
Nothing: only the track width matters
It rises, since a heavier vehicle is harder to tip
questions.explanation: The tipping acceleration is g times half the track over the height. Raising the height by two thirds cuts it by 40 percent.

questions.question: Why does an accelerometer alone give 27 degrees of roll in a steady turn on level ground?
options: Its gyro has drifted by 27 degrees
It feels the sideways acceleration of the turn as well as gravity and cannot tell them apart
The floor is tilted by that much
It is saturated by the vibration
questions.explanation: A sideways acceleration of 4 m/s2 with gravity looks exactly like gravity on a floor tilted by the arctangent of 4 over 9.81.

questions.question: Why did a gate of 15 percent of g not help in a turn at 4 m/s^2?
options: The gate was too tight and rejected every sample
The gyro's bias was too large
The magnitude is only about 8 percent over g, which is inside the gate
The vibration was larger than the turn
questions.explanation: The filter trusted the accelerometer. Gravity and 4 m/s2 at right angles have a size only 8 percent above g. A gate of 15 percent lets that through, and the error was 22.1 degrees against 5.1 at 3 percent.

questions.question: What did a gate of 1 percent cost?
options: Nothing: a tighter gate is always better
The gyro's bias built up because few samples passed
It followed the accelerometer into every turn
It stopped the robot in every turn
questions.explanation: 4.1 degrees after 60 s against 1.2 at 15 percent. Vibration moves the magnitude by about 3 percent, so a 1 percent gate rejects nearly everything and the gyro is rarely corrected.

questions.question: Why does the tilt monitor need a debounce on its stop level but not on its warning?
options: The warning level is reached less often
A warning is reported to the operator and a stop is not
A single bump past the stop level should not stop the robot, and a warning costs nothing to give early
The stop level is measured by a different sensor
questions.explanation: One sample over the stop level may be a bump. Three in a row is a tilt. A warning costs nothing, and a NaN is a stop at once.
